title: Protocol for the use of focused ion-beam milling to prepare crystalline lamellae for microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED)
protocol: Dissolve dry powder of lysozyme into a buffer of 0.1 M sodium acetate pH 4.8 solution to a concentration of 40 mg / mL.
Filter the protein solution through a 0.4 μm syringe filter at least 3 times.
Aliquot the protein into 50 μL portions in PCR tubes and flash freeze in liquid nitrogen.
Store aliquots at −80°C until just prior to use.
Thaw the protein on ice prior to experiments, and spin down the aliquots at 1–5,000 RPM on a tabletop centrifuge to remove aggregates.
Create a stock solution of 4 M NaCl using filtered water.
Filter the salt solution through a porous membrane at least 3 times.
Create a stock solution of 1 M sodium acetate pH 4.8 using filtered water.
Similarly filter to assure purity and remove aggregates.
Mix 1 mL of sodium acetate with 2.5 mL NaCl stock.
Add 6.5 mL of filtered water to the mixture.
Gently mix the solution to create a 1 M NaCl, 0.1 M sodium acetate pH 4.8 precipitant solution.
Mix 1–5 μL of protein stock solution with the precipitant solution in a PCR tube at a ratio of 1:1.
Gently mix the mixture with a pipette for 30 seconds.
Crystals form in 1–10 days at approximately 23°C.
Prepare TEM grids by applying the protein crystals to a glow discharged grid.
Blot away excess solvent from the grid.
Plunge the crystallized samples into liquid ethane.
Gently place the cover slide with the TEM grids into a glow discharge chamber and replace the cover to assure a vacuum-tight seal.
Glow discharge the grids on the negative setting for 10–30 seconds at a current of 15 mA.
Place the cover slide back into the glass petri dish.
Replace the glass cover to prevent dust or contamination from building up on the grids.
Use mountable forceps to grab a TEM grid by the outer edge, ensuring not to puncture the inner portion with the tips of the forceps.
Lock the forceps closed on the grid and place it into the vitrification robot.
Move the forceps into the sample chamber of the vitrification robot and allow the grid to equilibrate for approximately 1 minute.
Using a 10 μL pipette, place approximately 1–3 μL of solution containing crystals onto the carbon side of the TEM grid inside the vitrification robot sample chamber.
Wait 20 seconds and then blot the TEM grid gently from the back for approximately 20 seconds.
Cool down the dual beam transfer station to liquid nitrogen temperatures.
Transfer vitrified TEM grids from the vitrification robot chamber to the cooled dual beam transfer station.
Plunge blotted TEM grids into super-cooled liquid ethane for vitrification of crystals on the grid.
Transfer the prepared vitrified TEM grids to a grid storage box.
Prepare additional samples by repeating the blotting and vitrification process as needed.
Transfer grid boxes containing prepared grids into a liquid nitrogen storage dewar for long-term storage.
Design customized autogrid clips for FIB/SEM lamella preparation.
Ensure one side of the clip has a thinner edge for shallower milling angles.
Transfer grids into the dual beam shuttle for transfer into the FIB/SEM instrument.
Place the carbon side of the grid where crystals are facing outward.
Orient the clip ring toward the shallower side or appropriate identifier.
Mark an edge of the clip ring with a dot using a marker to identify orientation.
Load the grids inside the dual beam sample shuttle into the dual beam instrument.
Allow the dual beam instrument to return to optimal vacuum state after loading.
Apply a layer of platinum to the grids using the sputter coating system.
Perform a fine sputter coating at 1 kV and 7 mA for 30 seconds.
Perform a rough sputter coating at 1 kV and 30 mA for 30 seconds.
Increase nitrogen gas flow during the sputter coating process to prevent sample heating and ice contamination.
Screen loaded grids for appropriate crystals using an all-grid map or single image.
Use commercial software or the microscope’s positioning system to store positions on the stage where potential crystals are visible.
Identify crystals that are not on top of grid bars, not within 3 grid squares of the edge of the sample, and that are on unbroken/bend/ripped grid squares.
Bring each selected crystal to the eucentric tilting position.
Take a high-resolution image in both SEM and ion-beam to assure the beams are aligned to the same point at the specified milling angle.
Mill selected crystals into thin lamellae.
Rough mill away the bulk material from above and below the selected crystal using rectangular patterns.
Begin the fine milling process to slowly thin the rough lamella into a sharp edged slab.
Monitor the thickness during the fine milling process to ensure the specimen is not damaged due to beam drift.
Polish the lamella to the proper thickness and assure the lamella is perfectly flat.
Conduct polishing at ion beam currents of 1.5–30 pA using a cleaning cross section pattern.
Take a final image of the lamella using the ion-beam at high magnification and very low beam current.
Measure the final thickness of the polished lamella.
Monitor the milling progress using the scanning electron beam.
Check for dark, featureless bands in front of and behind the lamella to confirm successful milling.
Observe the lamella in the SEM to ensure no damage to crystalline order.
Repeat steps (a) – (d) for all selected crystals.
Limit the total number of crystals milled in a single session to perhaps 1–20.
Conduct milling steps in series for each lamella rather than finishing one complete before moving to the next.
Transfer grids with milled lamellae into a liquid nitrogen storage dewar until TEM is available for use.
Load grids directly into a cryo-cooled TEM without storing them for large periods of time.
Remove grids containing milled lamellae from storage dewar.
Load grids into cryogenically cooled TEM.
Carefully load grid into side entry holder or autoloading system with alpha tilt perpendicular to milling direction.
Screen loaded grids for milled lamella.
Take an all-grid atlas/montage of each sample.
Identify milled crystals by the clear stipe of missing material.
Add coordinates of each lamella to a list for further investigation.
Prepare the identified lamellae for data collection.
Take a high magnification image for each site.
Bring each site to the eucentric position if the lamella is not contaminated or broken.
Collect continuous rotation MicroED data from each lamella.
Remove the grids and either store them for future use or discard them as needed.
Convert continuous rotation MicroED movies into a standard crystallographic format using MicroED-tools.
Use command line on a Mac or Linux based system for simplicity.
Collect frames in TIF, MRC, SER, or other formats as specified by TEM detector software.
In this case, convert single MRC files containing continuous sweep data from one crystal to SMV format.
Ensure experimental parameters are correctly placed into each image header during conversion.
Index the MicroED data using standard crystallographic software.
Integrate the MicroED data using standard crystallographic software.
Determine the crystallographic space group using POINTLESS.
Scale and merge the data using AIMLESS.
Convert intensities to amplitudes using CTRUNCATE for downstream refinement programs.
Merge all seven crystals together using XSCALE.
Copy the R free set from the molecular replacement model to the new dataset in space group P43212.
Open the molecular replacement model and map to inspect the solution using COOT.
Refine the protein structure using electron scattering factors with PHENIX.
Add ordered solvent and ions to the structure as they appear in the density.
Repeat manual inspection of the maps between rounds of structure refinement until satisfied with the model.
